Ask ten drummers how to hold a stick and you'll get several answers, and most of them are
right. This lesson shows the common grips, why each exists, and then the other places
where good kit players do things differently. Its aim is to tell a choice from a mistake: a
choice suits a style or a body; a mistake causes pain or a choked sound in any style.

## What every grip shares

- **A fulcrum.** The stick pivots at one point, held between the thumb and a finger (the
  first or middle finger). About a third of the way up from the butt end is a usual starting
  place; slide it until the stick bounces most freely off a pad.
- **Rebound.** Let the stick come back up by itself. The hand guides it and doesn't fight it.
  Gripping hard kills the rebound, dulls the sound and tires the forearm.
- **Back fingers loose.** The other fingers wrap the stick lightly, never squeezing; there
  should be a little air between the palm and the stick.

## Matched grip

Both hands hold the stick the same way, palm roughly down. Most kit players today use it.
There are three named positions; they differ only in how far the hand is turned.

| Grip | Palms | Moves mostly with | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **German** | Flat, facing the floor; sticks about 90° apart | The wrist (up and down) | Volume, backbeats, big strokes |
| **American** | Turned about 45° | Wrist and fingers together | An all-round default, moving around the kit |
| **French** | Thumbs on top, palms facing each other | The fingers | Speed and finesse at low volume, cymbal work, jazz |

Most players move between them in a single song: closer to German for a loud backbeat,
closer to French for fast ride-cymbal patterns. Start with American.

## Traditional grip

The left hand (for a right-handed player) holds the stick differently: it sits in the web
between thumb and first finger, resting on the third finger, palm turned up; the
hand turns like turning a doorknob. It comes from marching drums slung at an angle on a
strap, where a matched left hand hit the tilted head awkwardly. It's still common in jazz and
drum corps for the light, controlled touch it gives the left hand, and many players simply
like how it feels.

Choose traditional grip if you want it, not because a style requires it: plenty of jazz
drummers play matched grip. It takes longer to learn, and the snare is usually tilted
toward the player to suit it.

## Stroke types

The grip matters less than the motion. Four strokes cover nearly everything:

- **Full stroke:** start high, strike, let it rebound back to high. Loud notes in a row.
- **Down stroke:** start high, strike, stop the stick low. An accent followed by a quiet note.
- **Tap:** start low, strike, return low. Quiet notes.
- **Up stroke:** start low, strike quietly, lift to high. A quiet note followed by an accent.

**Moeller** (after Sanford Moeller, a teacher of drum corps drummers) is a whipping motion of
the forearm, wrist and stick that gets an accent and a tap or two out of one throw. Many
drummers use something like it without the name.

## Other places drummers differ

| Choice | The options | What decides it |
|---|---|---|
| **Which hand leads** | Right-handed kit (hi-hat on the left, right hand crosses over to it), left-handed kit (a mirror image), or **open-handed** (right-handed kit, left hand plays the hi-hat, no crossing) | Comfort. Open-handed frees the right hand for the snare and toms; Billy Cobham and Simon Phillips play this way. |
| **Leading foot** | Bass drum on the right foot or the left | Usually the same side as the strong hand; a left-footed player often plays a left-handed kit. |
| **Bass drum pedal** | **Heel up** (on the ball of the foot, the leg does the work) or **heel down** (the ankle does it) | Heel up: power, rock. Heel down: control and quiet, jazz. Many players change in a song. |
| **Burying the beater** | Leave the beater against the head after a stroke, or let it bounce off | Buried: a short, punchy note. Off the head: a fuller, open note. |
| **Hi-hat foot** | Keep it closed, rock the foot heel-toe to keep time, or play it on 2 and 4 | Style. Jazz drummers often play the foot on 2 and 4. |
| **Throne height** | Thighs level or sloping slightly down to the knee | Higher gives power; lower gives a stable seat. Too low hurts the hips and lower back. |
| **Kit size** | Four pieces (kick, snare, one rack tom, floor tom) up to large kits | The music and the room. Four or five pieces is enough for most styles. |
| **Cymbal height and angle** | Flat and low, or high and tilted | Reach without stretching; flat for jazz ride playing, angled so the stick hits with the side of the tip, not the edge with the shoulder of the stick (which cracks cymbals). |
| **Sticks** | 7A (thin, light), 5A (the default), 5B and 2B (thick, heavy); wood or nylon tips | Volume and the hand. Nylon tips make a brighter cymbal sound. |
| **Matched or traditional** | See above | Taste. |
| **Reading and counting** | Read notation, count aloud, learn by ear | Most professionals do all three; the [Drum Set](../tools/drumset.qmd) page writes grooves in notation. |

## Signs of a mistake, not a choice

- Pain in the wrist, forearm or lower back. Stop, rest, and look at your grip and throne height.
- White knuckles, or the stick buzzing in a tight hand.
- Hitting rim and cymbal edges with the shaft of the stick (chipped sticks, cracked cymbals).
- Every stroke the same height: no accents and a flat sound.
- Reaching or leaning to play anything you play often.

## Practice

1. On a practice pad, play 8 full strokes per hand at a slow tempo with a metronome. Watch that
   each stick comes back to the height it started at.
2. Play the same 8 strokes in German, then American, then French grip. Listen for the change in sound.
3. Accents: alternate a down stroke and three taps (R L L L, then L R R R), then put them in a groove.
4. Try one foot setting you don't use: heel down if you play heel up, or the reverse.
